# Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

## The thesis, precisely

Alexis King's 2019 essay ["Parse, don't
validate"](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/)
is often reduced to "check inputs early," which misses its actual content. The
distinction is about **what happens to the knowledge a check produces**.

A *validator* in her sense is a function like `validateNonEmpty :: [a] -> ()`:
it inspects, throws on failure, and returns nothing. The knowledge that the
list was non-empty exists for one instant and is discarded; every later
consumer either trusts blindly or checks again. A *parser* is
`parseNonEmpty :: [a] -> NonEmpty a`: the same inspection, but the result is
recorded **in the type of the output**. Downstream code that receives a
`NonEmpty a` cannot even ask whether it is empty — the question has been
settled, permanently, by construction.

Two named pathologies follow from doing it the other way. **Shotgun parsing**
(a term from the language-theoretic security literature) is the anti-pattern
of scattering input checks throughout processing code, interleaved with the
processing itself — the program acts on input before fully deciding the input
is well-formed, and rejection paths can fire after side effects have already
happened. **Boolean blindness** (Robert Harper's coinage) is the information
loss of reducing a rich check to a `TRUE`/`FALSE`: the boolean remembers
*that* something was true but not *what* or *why*, so the evidence must be
reconstructed downstream — usually by checking again.

## The translation to a dynamic language

R has no compile-time types, so the slogan cannot mean "let the type checker
carry proofs." The translation is nonetheless faithful:

**A parser is a boundary function that returns a domain object or fails
loudly. Possession of the object is the proof.**

Concretely, with S7: construction runs property class checks, property
validators, and the class validator; every property replacement re-runs them.
Therefore *an S7 object of class `Color` that exists* is evidence that its
laws held at construction and after every legitimate modification since. A
function receiving a `Color` needs no defensive re-checking of channel ranges
— demanding the class (via dispatch or a property's declared class) *is* the
check. This is what "make illegal states unconstructable" buys: the object
functions as a certificate.

Honesty requires noting the seams in a dynamic language. R will not stop
someone from calling `attr()` surgery on the object's internals, and S7
itself ships named escape hatches: `S7::valid_eventually()` suspends
validation while a function runs and validates once at the end, while
`S7::valid_implicitly()` suspends it and performs *no* final check —
verified directly against S7 0.2.2: it will hand back an object that
violates its own class validator. A getter can likewise return output that
violates its declared class (getter output is not auto-validated). The
guarantee is therefore conventional, and the precise phrasing matters:
**construction through the supported API is the runtime certificate**, and
it certifies only the laws actually encoded. Mutate through the front door —
constructors, `@<-`, `S7::set_props()`, exported mutator functions — and the
certificate holds. Package design reinforces the convention by exporting
only the front door, and treats `valid_implicitly()` as what it is: an
internal performance tool whose caller assumes the burden of proof.

## Constructors parse; validators verify

The clean division of labor inside an S7 class:

**Constructors (and boundary functions) normalize.** They accept the messy
input the outside world actually produces — a hex string or a channel array;
a double `8` where an integer is meant; a bare scalar where a list is
expected — and either produce canonical property values or abort with a
user-facing error that names the argument (this is where
`cli::cli_abort()` with `rlang::caller_arg()` context belongs). Coercion,
canonicalization, and version gating are all *parsing* and all happen here,
once.

**Validators verify canonical values.** By the time a validator runs, its
input should already be in the one true representation; the validator's job
is to *reject unlawful values*, not to accommodate alternative shapes. A
property validator that tolerates five input forms "for convenience" is a
parser wearing a validator's clothes — and since validators run on every
construction *and every property replacement*, it re-runs its accommodation
logic forever, on values that were already clean.

This is also Postel's law put in its correct place: be liberal in what you
accept **at the boundary parser**, and conservative everywhere else. The core
of a well-built system is strict precisely because the boundary was generous.

## The checking ladder

Every check in a system has exactly one correct home. The rungs, from the
outside world inward:

**Rung 0 — external conformance validators.** Full wire-format conformance —
JSON Schema via AJV, an official specification validator, a database's own
constraint engine — belongs to the authority that owns the specification.
Re-implementing an external spec's full semantics inside property validators
is expensive, drift-prone duplication. Published S7 packages are consistent on
this: S7schema delegates YAML/JSON conformance to AJV; stacbuildr validates
catalogs against the published STAC schemas; a style-document package should
shell out to the official style validator for whole-document conformance.
These run **once, at the wire**, not on every property write.

**Rung 1 — boundary parsers.** `from_json()`, `read_as_markdown()`,
`color_hex()`: loose input in, domain objects out, `cli`-formatted errors
with caller context on failure. All coercion lives here.

**Rung 2 — property class.** The declared class (possibly a union with
`NULL`) is the base type check. S7 runs it before the property validator, so
validators may assume the type.

**Rung 3 — property validator.** Local laws of one value: scalar-ness,
length, range, set membership, pattern. Pure, cheap, no knowledge of any
other property. Returns `NULL` or one message (without the property name —
S7 prepends it, which is what makes property definitions reusable).

**Rung 4 — setters.** Normalization-on-write for meaning-preserving cleanup
only. Used sparingly; a setter making semantic decisions is doing rung 1's or
rung 5's job invisibly.

**Rung 5 — class validator.** Laws relating several properties of one
object: ordering (`start <= end`), mutual exclusion, conditional
requiredness. Receives `self`, returns `NULL` or a character vector of
problems, refers to properties as `@name`. Must not repeat rungs 2–3.

**Rung 6 — aggregate validator.** Laws relating *several objects* in a
containing structure: unique ids across a collection, references that must
resolve, pairings between siblings. These belong to the **lowest class that
can see everything the law mentions** — usually a root document object. This
is Eric Evans's *aggregate* from domain-driven design: the consistency
boundary, whose root is the only thing outsiders hold and through which all
modification flows. An invariant placed *below* its visibility horizon cannot
be checked; placed *above* it, it runs too often and knows too much.

**Rung 7 — operation preconditions.** Some states are lawful to *be in* but
unlawful to *reach by a particular operation*: adding a source whose id
already exists, removing a source that layers still reference. These are
workflow rules, not document laws — the document containing the source was
always valid — so they live in the mutator functions (`add_source()`,
`remove_source()`), erroring with `cli::cli_abort()` before any modification.

**Rung 8 — internal assertions.** Developer-facing checks for states the
maintainer believes impossible, kept while refactoring, never part of the
user contract.

Each rung **assumes all rungs below it and duplicates none of them.** The
most common failure of validation architecture is not a missing check but the
same law encoded on three rungs, which triples the maintenance surface and
guarantees the encodings eventually disagree. When you find a law with two
homes, delete one — or, more precisely, designate one home as
*authoritative*. A deliberately retained cheap duplicate (a boundary check
restating an inner law to produce a faster, better-localized error message)
is a legitimate trade, provided it is documented as a duplicate and the
authoritative rung is named. What the rule forbids is accidental
multiplicity, where nobody knows which encoding governs.

## The cost model

Validators are not free, and their cost profile is part of the design.
Property and class validators run at every construction and every property
replacement — they are the *hot path* of the object system. Hence:

- Validators must be **pure** (no I/O, no network, no reads of global state)
  and **fast** (no quadratic scans where avoidable).
- Expensive conformance — full-document schema validation, cross-document
  consistency, anything touching disk — belongs on rungs 0–1, which run once
  per boundary crossing.
- If an aggregate's rung-6 validator becomes genuinely expensive (huge
  collections revalidated on every append), that is a signal to provide bulk
  constructors and batch mutators (build the whole collection, validate once)
  rather than to weaken the validator. S7 supplies the sanctioned mechanism:
  `S7::valid_eventually(x, fun)` suspends validation for the duration of
  `fun` and validates once at the end — a transaction in the literal sense,
  verified to pass through transient-invalid intermediate states and still
  reject an unlawful final state.

There is also a subtle *transactionality* consequence: because validation
fires per replacement, invariants spanning multiple properties require atomic
multi-property updates (`S7::set_props()`), or legitimate transitions will be
rejected mid-flight. This was developed in
[02-values-and-state.qmd](02-values-and-state.qmd).

## The time axis: as early as possible, as late as necessary

The ladder places checks in *space* — which layer owns which law. Checks also
have a placement in *time*, and the rule has two halves.

**Shift left when the check needs nothing you don't already have.** The rtemis
framework demonstrates both extremes of this. At the earliest possible moment:
its property factories validate the *declaration itself* — a declared default
outside its own declared bounds, or a double default on an integer property,
"fails at factory time — i.e. at package load — rather than at first
instantiation." The author's mistake surfaces before any user exists. At the
last moment before expense: its `setup_*()` functions construct fully
validated configuration objects *before* a training run that may fit
thousands of models, so a typo in a hyperparameter costs milliseconds instead
of hours. Both are the same principle: the value of a check is proportional to
the cost of the work it gates, and it should run as far before that work as
its inputs allow. A validated configuration object is itself a
parse-don't-validate move — the certificate is minted at setup time and
trusted at run time.

**Defer when the law mentions context that does not exist yet.** Some
constraints cannot be checked at construction because they relate the value to
something external: rtemis's `data_bound` properties declare that a
hyperparameter is constrained by a *training-data dimension* (`mtry` bounded
by the number of features; per-case weights matching the number of rows;
feature selections that must be a subset of the column names). These are
declared as data on the property and resolved in one pass, against the data,
immediately before training begins — not smuggled into a validator that would
have to guess, and not silently skipped. The general form: when a law spans
the object and its eventual context, *declare* it at construction time and
*check* it at the first moment the context is in hand, in one named place.

## Errors as values: the second channel

R's condition system is a control-flow channel: an error unwinds the stack
until something catches it. There is a second, complementary discipline in
which failure travels through the *data* flow instead — the `Result`/`Option`
family from Rust and the ML lineage — and the
[resultr](https://github.com/TransGirlCodes/resultr) package shows it is a
natural fit for S7. `Result` is an abstract class existing purely for
dispatch; `Success` and `Failure` are one-property variants; the combinator
vocabulary (`unwrap()`, `unwrap_or_else()`, `and_then()`, `expect()`) is a
set of generics with per-variant methods. The `Failure` method for
`and_then()` just returns itself — which is the entire "railway-oriented
programming" pattern in one line: once a pipeline is on the failure track,
every subsequent step passes the failure through untouched, and the caller
inspects the outcome once, at the end.

The architectural point is not "use Result everywhere"; conditions remain the
right channel for *bugs and contract violations* (a validator rejecting an
unlawful value should absolutely throw). Values are the right channel when
**failure is an expected outcome the caller will branch on as data** — a
batch of items where some fail and the survivors matter; a fallible lookup
feeding a pipeline that should complete. What resultr gets exactly right is
the conversion discipline: its `wrap_in_result()` generic converts conditions
into values at *one designed point* (methods on `class_error` and
`class_warning` wrap into `Failure`; everything else into `Success`; a
`Result` passes through), inside a single `rlang::try_fetch()`. Two channels,
one explicit adapter between them — never ad hoc `tryCatch` scattered through
the middle of the system. It also enforces its certificates: the `@value` and
`@error` properties use write-once setters that error on reassignment, making
the outcome tamper-evident.

## Conditions: errors as a designed surface

R's condition system is unusually rich — conditions are classed, structured,
signalable, catchable by class, and chainable — and a domain package should
treat its error behavior as designed API, not incidental output. A workable
stratification, aligned with the ladder:

**User errors** (rungs 1 and 7): the caller did something fixable. These
deserve the full treatment — `cli::cli_abort()` with a message naming the
argument (`rlang::caller_arg()`), attributed to the calling frame
(`rlang::caller_env()`) so the error points at the user's code rather than
package internals, with a `parent =` chain when wrapping a lower-level
failure. Message content should say what was expected, what arrived, and when
possible what to do.

**Invariant violations** (rungs 3, 5, 6): terse declarative strings returned
from validators — "must be between 0 and 255" — which S7 assembles into its
own error, prefixing property names. These are not the place for `cli`
markup or call-site attribution; they are law statements.

**Warnings**: recoverable degradation the caller should know about but need
not stop for — a deprecated field mapped forward, a lossy normalization
applied. Never use a warning where the result is unusable.

**Progress and information**: `cli` messaging in the shell, never in the
core. A constructor that chatters is a constructor that cannot be used in a
pipeline.

Classed conditions earn their keep the moment any caller needs to *handle*
one failure differently from another: give programmatically distinguishable
failures their own condition classes rather than making callers grep message
text.

## Design by contract, and making it testable

Bertrand Meyer's design-by-contract vocabulary maps cleanly onto this
architecture and is worth using in design discussions. **Preconditions** are
rungs 1 and 7 — what must be true for the operation to proceed, the caller's
responsibility. **Invariants** are rungs 3, 5, 6 — what is always true of a
lawful object, the class's responsibility. **Postconditions** are the
guarantees of the return value — largely carried by the returned *type*
(parse-don't-validate again: the strongest postcondition is "returns a
`Color`"), plus documented promises like "the result's getter outputs conform
to their declared classes," which S7 leaves on the author's honor.

The contracts become *testable* in two complementary ways. Ordinary example
tests exercise each rung: construction succeeds on lawful input, each unlawful
input is rejected *by the right rung* with the right message, mutation through
the front door revalidates, round-trips are identities. And **law-based
(property-based) testing** generalizes them: state algebraic laws the domain
must satisfy — serialization round-trips, order-insensitivity of collection
construction, idempotence of normalization — and test them against generated
inputs. The s7contract package packages exactly this for S7: explicit
interface declarations (required generics), traits with registered
implementations, optional runtime argument/return checking, and generative
laws with shrinking. Whether or not one adopts the package, the mindset — an
interface is a set of generics *plus laws*, and laws are executable — is the
mature endpoint of validation thinking.

## The payoff, restated

When the ladder is respected, a characteristic calm settles over the middle
of the codebase. Core functions take domain objects and return domain
objects; they contain no `if (!is.character(x))` boilerplate, because rungs
below them already settled it; their tests test logic, not plumbing. All the
suspicion concentrates at the edges, where it belongs, in a small number of
parsers with excellent error messages. The system's trust structure becomes
legible: you can point at any function and say exactly what it is entitled to
assume and which rung guarantees it.
